title: The Hot Dish and the Laminated Plan

pages.text:
At 8:05, the doorbell rang, and I did not move.

Mrs. Abernathy was tiny. She wore a floral gardening hat that looked like it had survived a hurricane, and she carried a glass dish so heavy it bowed her shoulders. Tuna noodle casserole. Potato chips on top, arranged in a perfect, crunchy roof.

"It's a hot dish, so be careful," she said, her voice thin and sweet. "You'll want a trivet."

I looked at the chips. I looked at her hands, which were spotted and strong. I said nothing. I was busy being the worst person in the house, and silence was part of the plan.

Dad stepped out of the kitchen, still holding a burnt slice of toast. He beamed.

"Thank you, Mrs. A," he said. Then, louder, as if volume could cure my rudeness: "THANK YOU, MRS. A. That is wonderful."

She smiled, a little stiffly, and placed the dish on the counter. The chips crunched under the weight. I felt a tiny, stupid spike of guilt, but I ignored it. Guilt was a luxury for people who liked things. I was in the business of ruining them.
pages.image: Mrs. Abernathy, a tiny elderly woman in a floral hat, places a heavy glass dish of casserole on a kitchen counter while Dad, a large man in a fish apron, smiles broadly behind her.

pages.text:
My phone buzzed on the floor at 8:30, the blue light cutting through the dim room like a flashlight in a dark closet. I stared at the screen. It was Jonah.

"I HAVE A PLAN. Be at my house at 2. Wear shoes you can get wet."

I typed the word *maybe* and looked at it, but it felt weak, like a door left ajar. I deleted it and turned the phone face down.

You should know about Jonah Park. We have been best friends since kindergarten, which means I have seen him fall off a swing set, cry at a dog movie, and once explain why the moon was "looking at him" during a math test. He wears a bike helmet everywhere, always, to the library, the ice cream shop, and even his own bedroom. It is not a joke. It is a lifestyle.

Last summer, we built a raft out of pool noodles and a tarp, and we pushed it into the creek. It sank in eight inches of water. Jonah did not get angry. He just said, "Okay, that was a learning moment," and we went home to get dry socks.

I wanted to go. I really, really wanted to go. But I was the person who had lost, and losers don't go to parties.
pages.image: Max lies on the floor, staring at a smartphone lying face down, while Jonah Park, a boy in a bike helmet, looks on from the doorway with a huge grin.

pages.text:
At 9:15, the world almost ended.

Dad carried a box marked FRAGILE/KITCHEN in thick red marker. His grip slipped, or his elbow hit the doorframe, or gravity simply decided to be unhelpful. The box fell.

Time never slows down, but it felt like it did. I watched the box tumble through the air. I saw Dad’s face go white. I saw Mom, standing by the pantry with her clipboard, drop her pencil.

She dove.

It wasn't a swimmer's dive. It was the way a dog catches a frisbee. Her body stretched out, her hands shot forward, and she caught the box a hand-span from the hardwood floor. The plates inside rattled, a sound like rain on a tin roof.

Silence followed, thick and heavy, until one by one, we started to laugh. It was the nervous, shaking kind you get when you think you’ve failed but you haven’t.

I did not laugh. I stood in the middle of the room, arms crossed, feeling heavy and still.

"Max," Mom said. She was breathing hard. Her hair was falling out of her clip. She didn’t bother fixing it. "Please. Just today."

"Just today is all I've got left," I said.

I hated how it sounded. It was a line from a movie. I turned and walked out of the kitchen.
pages.image: Mom dives to catch a falling cardboard box, her arms outstretched, while Dad and Max stand frozen in the background, Max looking stern and Mom looking breathless.

pages.text:
I retreated to the garage, which was half-empty too.

Just the car, a ladder, and boxes. I walked past the ladder and stopped in front of the last one. It was small, holding Tessa’s drum practice pad, old Kettle Drums posters, and my soccer trophies. My gold cup for the regional finals stuck out the top, gleaming in the dusty light.

"Hey."

I turned. Tessa stood in the doorway, her purple streak pulled back, headphones around her neck, and drumsticks in her back pocket. She looked at the box. Then she looked at me.

"That's mine," she said.

"It's in the middle of the room," I replied. "I'm moving it."

"You're moving everything," she said, her voice flat and cold. "You think you're the only one this is happening to?"

I looked at her, then at the posters. I saw the name *Kettle Drums* on one. I knew exactly what to say. It was the easiest thing to reach, the sharpest tool I had.

"You don't have anyone to play for anyway," I said. "No friends. Just the drums."

Her face went still. Not angry. Just paused, like a video game waiting for input.

She stared at me for a long second. Then she turned and walked out. The garage door slammed shut behind her, a sound like a gunshot.
pages.image: Max stands in a dusty garage holding a box, while Tessa, a teenage girl with a purple hair streak, turns to leave with her back to him, looking rigid and silent.

pages.text:
I stood in the garage, listening to the refrigerator hum through the wall. The light was dim, and my own heartbeat felt loud enough to rattle the boxes around me. What I’d said was the meanest thing I’d ever said to anyone, and it was true, which made it worse. I had chosen it because it was the sharpest tool I had, reaching for the knife without checking who was holding it.

I sat down on the cold concrete, pulling my knees up to my chest. Upstairs, through the floorboards, came a rhythm. Tap. Tap. Tap-tap-tap. Fast, then suddenly stopped. The silence that followed was heavier than the noise. I waited, not knowing if I was hoping for an apology, a scream, or for the door to open and Tessa to tell me to get lost. Nothing happened.

Then the doorbell rang.

It was 11:00. I didn’t need to check my phone to know who was there. I could see the round shape of a bike helmet on the front step, just visible through the window glass.
pages.image: Max sits on the garage floor hugging his knees, looking up at the closed garage door, his expression lonely and regretful.
